name: Dental evulsion

lead: Dental evulsion, also called tooth ablation, is the deliberate removal of healthy teeth, usually front teeth, as a mark of identity, beauty, or passage into adulthood, marriage or mourning. It has been recorded in many ancient and modern societies across Africa, Asia and Oceania.

Its appearance effect is the point: the gap is highly visible and signals membership. In some groups a lower lip plate is paired with extraction of lower front teeth, and removing lower teeth can visibly change facial features and speech.

paras: Traditions are carried out within communities, not as a consumer practice. Methods recorded include knocking teeth out with a stick and stone in Hawaii and using a fine blade among the Nuer, with no anesthetic. Among Nilotic peoples in South Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania it is a long-standing custom, and in some areas it persists as a teenage rite.

Every method involves pain and risk of infection. Tooth loss can alter how remaining teeth emerge, how the jaws meet and how teeth wear, and can affect speech sounds. In South Africa, dentists have fitted thousands of partial dentures for people wanting a conventional smile.

angle.text: In the societies that practice it, the changed smile is the intended aesthetic and social signal. It is recorded here as a cultural tradition and its harms are documented below.

lead: Tooth ablation, also called tooth evulsion, is the deliberate removal of healthy teeth. It has been recorded in many ancient and modern societies, where it marks group identity, adds ornamentation, or serves as a rite of passage tied to coming of age, marriage or mourning. The social meaning for ancient populations is described as likely to remain unknown [1].

Regional traditions include East and East Central Africa, where it is mainly a Nilotic custom (Dinka, Nuer, Maban, Luo, Maasai); Central Sulawesi, where the Uma removed girls' incisors at puberty until the Dutch colonial government banned it around the 1920s; and Hawaii, the Marquesas and Aboriginal Australia, where it was linked to puberty and mourning [1].

The practice is relevant to appearance because it is immediately visible and defines a culturally recognised look. In some African groups, a lower lip plate is usually combined with extraction of two, sometimes four, lower front teeth [2].
infobox: Tooth ablation, tooth evulsion, tooth avulsion

paras: Methods vary but all involve pain and risk of infection. In Hawaii, incisors were knocked out with a stick and rock, often leaving roots in the jaw. In Sudan and the Upper Nile, fish hooks, metal wire or iron spikes were used, and the Nuer still use a fine blade without anesthetic [1].

In Africa the practice was once common in East and East Central Africa, and in Cape Town it occurs as a teenage rite in some low-income communities [1]. In Asia it is recorded in Central Sulawesi, eastern Guizhou, French Indochina, Sumatra, northern Formosa and Borneo; in Borneo it was tied to magical-religious beliefs [1].

In Oceania it was practiced in the Marquesas, in Hawaii on the death of a tribal leader, among Aboriginal Australian groups for puberty and mourning, and in the New Hebrides, where girls' upper central incisors were removed at puberty [1].

Lip plates are clay or wooden discs inserted in a pierced, gradually stretched lip. Wikipedia states that a lower lip plate is usually combined with extraction of two lower front teeth, sometimes all four, and among the Mursi and Surma of Ethiopia the plate is typically worn after a piercing begun in adolescence [2]. Anthropologist Shauna LaTosky links the plates to female strength and self-esteem [2].

Removal of lower teeth can visibly change facial features and affect speech sounds, and tooth loss can alter the emergence, occlusion and wear of remaining teeth [1]. Lip plates are associated with infection during piercing, difficulty eating, gum irritation and disease, tooth gaps and erosion, and the Ethiopian government has pushed to suppress the practice [2].

No studies found. Dental trauma literature covers accidental tooth avulsion, which is a separate topic: reviews describe it as a severe injury, note that replantation is common but with high failure rates and unpredictable long-term outcomes, and emphasise timely management [3][4].

timeline.event: Dutch colonial government bans the Uma practice of removing girls' incisors in Central Sulawesi (around this decade) [1].
